newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH - Hanson not the only cause of govt poll decline.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH - Hanson not the only cause of govt poll decline.

text.p: Populist MP Pauline Hanson is not the only reason why the government is losing voter support.
Hanson, who has lured some voters away with her campaign against Asian immigration and aboriginal welfare, should be affecting only the primary-vote measure of government support.

But Prime Minister John Howard is rapidly losing ground on the two-party measure, in which all voter support is distributed between the government and opposition, as it is in almost every seat in an election under the preferential voting system.
PRIMARY POLLING NO MYSTERY

The primary vote picture is well understood: Asked who would get their number-one vote under the preferential voting system, fewer respondents are nominating the government than a couple of months ago and fewer are nominating the opposition.
As analysed by the Reuters Poll Trend, the Liberal-National government has lost about seven percent of voters in recent months and the Labor opposition has lost one or two percent.
Allowing for a little loss from other parties, this seems to account for the roughly 10 percent support gathered by Hanson.
So One Nation seems to have picked up more former Liberal-National supporters than Labor supporters, and the government's lead over the opposition has therefore fallen.
BUT THE TWO-PARTY GROUND IS ALSO MOVING
Hanson should not affect the two-party picture.
In an Australian federal election, voters number the candidates in each seat in order of desirability.

If none of the candidates has 50 percent of the number-one votes, the least supported candidates are progressively eliminated and their votes reallocated according to the preference numbers until someone has a majority.
Since the top two candidates are almost always from the government and opposition, the votes for minor candidates are usually only important for their preferences.
A voter can back a Monster Raving Loony Party if he or she wishes, but the vote will eventually go to one of the big-two and the crucial issue is which of them has the highest preference.
The polls pick this up by asking the supporters of minor parties to nominate their preferred big party and the result is the so-called two-party measure of voter support.

Now imagine a voter abandoning the Liberal Party for Hanson's One Nation. This person would now give the number one vote (that is, primary support) to One Nation but, presumably, the number-two vote goes to the Liberals, so two-party support is unaffected.

But government two-party support is falling. On the Reuters Poll Trend, Howard's administration is now only about four points ahead of Labor on this measure, compared with the eight or nine points typical of the past few months.
So two things must be happening:
--Voters are leaving the government for Hanson, and also switching their major-party leanings to Labor.
--Supporters of other minority parties are switching their major-party leanings to Labor.
Certainly Hanson is drawing voters away from the big parties. But this development shows that the government must be driving them away, too.
Howard himself thinks they are disappointed.
"There were enormous expectations (on the government) as there are when you have a government replacing a government that's been in power for a long period of time," he told reporters on Tuesday.
"And I know there are some people out there who voted for us in March of last year who would have liked to have seen more change (so far).
"But the changes that we have brought about are working their way through the economy, particularly in areas like small business.
"And I think the real benefits of them will begin to be felt towards the end of this year ..."
Certainly, people elected Howard last year because they wanted improvements, and the unemployment rate alone shows that results so far have been modest (as one would expect).
But there are other factors, notably the government's support for smeared independent senator Mal Colston.
